results.title: Centre of the Frattini subgroup
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An element $x$ of a group $G$ lies in the centre $Z(\Phi(G))$ of the Frattini subgroup $\Phi(G)$ when $x \in \Phi(G)$ and $xy = yx$ for every $y \in \Phi(G)$.

results.title: Vanishing first cohomology of $G/\Phi(G)$ in $Z(\Phi(G))$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a group, let $\Phi(G)$ be its Frattini subgroup and let $Z(\Phi(G))$ be the centre of $\Phi(G)$. The property holds when every map $\delta \colon G \to Z(\Phi(G))$ with $\delta(gh) = \delta(g)\, g\, \delta(h)\, g^{-1}$ for all $g, h \in G$ and $\delta(g) = 1$ for all $g \in \Phi(G)$ is a coboundary: there is an $a \in Z(\Phi(G))$ with $\delta(g) = g a g^{-1} a^{-1}$ for all $g \in G$.

results.title: Class of groups
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A class of groups, as a predicate on groups in `Type`.

results.title: Formations of groups in the sense of Gaglione and Spellman
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A class $\mathfrak{F}$ of groups is a formation when it contains at least one group, it is closed under surjective homomorphic images (if $G \in \mathfrak{F}$ and $\varphi \colon G \to H$ is a surjective homomorphism, then $H \in \mathfrak{F}$), and for every group $G$ and all normal subgroups $N_1$, $N_2$ of $G$, if $G/N_1$ and $G/N_2$ lie in $\mathfrak{F}$, then so does $G/(N_1 \cap N_2)$.

results.title: First-order axiomatizable classes of groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A class $\mathfrak{F}$ of groups is first-order axiomatizable when there is a theory $T$ in the first-order language of groups such that a group $G$ lies in $\mathfrak{F}$ if and only if $G$, with its canonical structure, is a model of $T$.

results.title: Varieties of groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A class $\mathfrak{F}$ of groups is a variety when there is a set $W$ of elements of the free group on generators $x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$ such that a group $G$ lies in $\mathfrak{F}$ if and only if every $w \in W$ evaluates to $1$ in $G$ under every assignment of elements of $G$ to the generators.

results.title: The Gaglione–Spellman question on axiomatizable formations (Kourovka 14.32)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proposition that every first-order axiomatizable formation of groups is a variety: every class $\mathfrak{F}$ of groups that is a formation and is first-order axiomatizable is a variety.

results.title: Not every axiomatizable formation of groups is a variety
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Gaglione–Spellman question (Kourovka 14.32) has a negative answer: it is not the case that every first-order axiomatizable formation of groups is a variety, that is, some class of groups is a formation and is first-order axiomatizable but is not a variety.

results.title: Finite unramified intermediate fields
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $L/K$ a field extension such that the map $A \to L$ factors as $A \to K \to L$. An intermediate field $E$ of $L/K$ is finite unramified relative to $A$ if $E$ is finite-dimensional over $K$ and the integral closure of $A$ in $E$ is formally unramified over $A$.

results.title: Maximal unramified subextension
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $L/K$ a field extension such that the map $A \to L$ factors as $A \to K \to L$. The maximal unramified subextension of $L/K$ relative to $A$ is the supremum, in the lattice of intermediate fields of $L/K$, of all intermediate fields of $L/K$ that are finite unramified relative to $A$.

results.title: Finite unramified subfields lie in the maximal unramified subextension
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $L/K$ a field extension such that the map $A \to L$ factors as $A \to K \to L$. Every intermediate field $E$ of $L/K$ that is finite unramified relative to $A$ is contained in the maximal unramified subextension of $L/K$ relative to $A$.

results.title: Universal property of the maximal unramified subextension
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $L/K$ a field extension such that the map $A \to L$ factors as $A \to K \to L$. An intermediate field $F$ of $L/K$ contains the maximal unramified subextension of $L/K$ relative to $A$ if and only if $F$ contains every intermediate field of $L/K$ that is finite unramified relative to $A$.

results.title: Automorphisms preserve finite unramified subfields
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $L/K$ a field extension such that the map $A \to L$ factors as $A \to K \to L$. If an intermediate field $E$ of $L/K$ is finite unramified relative to $A$, then for every $K$-algebra automorphism $\sigma$ of $L$ the image $\sigma(E)$ is finite unramified relative to $A$.

results.title: The maximal unramified subextension is stable under automorphisms
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a commutative ring and $L/K$ a field extension such that the map $A \to L$ factors as $A \to K \to L$, and let $M$ be the maximal unramified subextension of $L/K$ relative to $A$. For every $K$-algebra automorphism $\sigma$ of $L$, $\sigma(M) = M$.

results.title: Sums invariant under a fixed-point-free involution are even
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a finite subset of a type $\alpha$, let $f : \alpha \to \alpha$ satisfy $f(a) \in s$, $f(f(a)) = a$ and $f(a) \neq a$ for every $a \in s$, and let $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{Z}$ satisfy $g(f(a)) = g(a)$ for every $a \in s$. results.title: Half a sum of even numbers modulo 2
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $s$ be a finite set of natural numbers and let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ be a function such that $f(k)$ is even for every $k \in s$. results.title: Odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers times the golden ratio
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $F_n$ be the Fibonacci numbers ($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$, $F_{n+2} = F_{n+1} + F_n$) and $\varphi = (1 + \sqrt 5)/2$ the golden ratio. For every natural number $k$, $F_{2k+1} \varphi = F_{2k+2} + \left((\sqrt 5 - 1)/2\right)^{2k+1}$ and $F_{2k+1} (1 + \varphi) = F_{2k+3} + \left((\sqrt 5 - 1)/2\right)^{2k+1}$.

results.title: Numeration by odd-indexed Fibonacci numbers
results.caption: Theorem

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every marked Dyck path $P$, the size of $P$ equals $N(P) + 2N^*(P)$, where $N(P)$ and $N^*(P)$ are the numbers of unmarked and marked vertical steps of $P$.

results.title: Steps of a multi-marked Dyck path
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A step of a multi-marked Dyck path is one of the horizontal step $E = (1, 0)$, the plain vertical step $N = (0, 1)$, or, for an integer $t \ge 2$, the marked vertical step $N^*_t = (0, 1)$ of index $t$. There are no marked steps of index less than $2$.

results.title: Number of horizontal steps in a multi-marked step sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ in $P$.

results.title: Number of plain vertical steps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), $N(P)$ is the number of plain (unmarked) vertical steps $N$ in $P$.

results.title: Number of vertical steps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), this is the number of vertical steps in $P$, plain steps $N$ and marked steps $N^*_t$ counted together.

results.title: Number of steps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_t$ with index $t \ge 2$), this is the total number of steps in $P$, that is, the length of $P$.

results.title: Index sum of a multi-marked step sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path, the index sum of $s$ is the sum of the indices $t$ over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$, each occurrence counted separately; the steps $E$ and $N$ contribute nothing.

results.title: Shifted index sum of a multi-marked step sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path, the shifted index sum of $s$ is the sum of $t - 1$ over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$, each occurrence counted separately; the steps $E$ and $N$ contribute nothing.

results.title: Number of marked steps of a given index
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite sequence $P$ of multi-marked steps (horizontal steps $E$, plain vertical steps $N$ and marked vertical steps $N^*_s$ with index $s \ge 2$) and a natural number $t$, $N^*_t(P)$ is the number of marked steps in $P$ whose index is exactly $t$.

results.title: Size of a multi-marked step sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The size of a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path is $E(s) + \sum (t - 1)$, where $E(s)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ in $s$ and the sum runs over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $s$.

results.title: Multi-marked Dyck path
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A multi-marked Dyck path is a finite sequence $P$ of steps, each a horizontal step $E = (1,0)$, a plain vertical step $N = (0,1)$ or a marked vertical step $N^*_t = (0,1)$ carrying an index $t \ge 2$, such that every prefix of $P$, including the empty prefix and $P$ itself, has at most as many vertical steps (plain and marked) as horizontal steps, and $P$ has exactly as many vertical steps as horizontal steps.

results.title: Equal horizontal and vertical step counts
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every multi-marked Dyck path $P$, the number $E(P)$ of horizontal steps of $P$ equals the number of vertical steps of $P$, plain steps $N$ and marked steps $N^*_t$ counted together.

results.title: Vertical count plus shifted index sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path, the number of vertical steps of $s$ plus the shifted index sum of $s$ equals the number of plain vertical steps $N$ of $s$ plus the index sum of $s$.

results.title: Two expressions for the size of a multi-marked Dyck path
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every multi-marked Dyck path $P$, the size $E(P) + \sum (t - 1)$ of $P$ equals $N(P) + \sum t$, where $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps $E$ of $P$, $N(P)$ is the number of plain vertical steps $N$ of $P$, and both sums run over all occurrences of marked steps $N^*_t$ in $P$.

results.title: Vertical steps of a multi-marked Dyck path
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A step of a multi-marked Dyck path is vertical when it is the plain step $N$ or a marked step $N^*_t$; the horizontal step $E$ is not vertical. This test delimits the final run of vertical steps of a step sequence.

results.title: Final run of vertical steps
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The final run of vertical steps of a finite sequence $s$ of steps of a multi-marked Dyck path is the longest suffix of $s$ consisting of vertical steps ($N$ or $N^*_t$): the part of $s$ after its last horizontal step $E$, or all of $s$ if $s$ has no step $E$.

results.title: Marked tail
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A multi-marked Dyck path $P$ has a marked tail when its final run of vertical steps (the steps after its last horizontal step $E$, or all of $P$ if $P$ has no step $E$) contains a marked vertical step $N^*_t$ for some index $t \ge 2$.

results.title: Unmarked tail
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A multi-marked Dyck path $P$ has an unmarked tail when it does not have a marked tail, that is, when its final run of vertical steps (the steps after its last horizontal step $E$, or all of $P$ if $P$ has no step $E$) contains no marked vertical step.

results.title: Multi-marked Dyck paths of a given size
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\tilde P_n$ is the set of multi-marked Dyck paths $P$ of size $n$. Here the size of $P$ is $E(P) + \sum (t - 1)$, where $E(P)$ is the number of horizontal steps of $P$ and the sum runs over the marked steps $N^*_t$ of $P$, each occurrence counted separately.

results.title: Multi-marked Dyck paths with an unmarked tail
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, $\tilde R_n$ is the set of multi-marked Dyck paths of size $n$ with an unmarked tail, that is, whose final run of vertical steps contains no marked step.

results.title: Chain cover
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a partially ordered set. A finite set $C$ of finite subsets of $\alpha$ is a chain cover of $\alpha$ when every member of $C$ is a chain and every element of $\alpha$ lies in some member of $C$.

results.title: Maximum antichain size
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite partially ordered set $\alpha$, the maximum antichain size of $\alpha$ (its width) is the largest number of elements of an antichain in $\alpha$.

results.title: Minimum chain cover size
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite partially ordered set $\alpha$, the minimum chain cover size of $\alpha$ is the smallest number of chains in a chain cover of $\alpha$, that is, in a finite set of chains of $\alpha$ whose union is $\alpha$.

results.title: Antichains are no larger than the maximum antichain size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially ordered set. Every antichain $A$ in $\alpha$ has at most as many elements as the maximum antichain size of $\alpha$.

results.title: Chain covers bound the minimum chain cover size
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially ordered set. If $C$ is a chain cover of $\alpha$, that is, a finite set of chains of $\alpha$ whose union is $\alpha$, then the minimum chain cover size of $\alpha$ is at most the number of chains in $C$.

results.title: Dilworth's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially ordered set. The maximum antichain size of $\alpha$ equals its minimum chain cover size: the largest number of elements of an antichain in $\alpha$ equals the smallest number of chains whose union is $\alpha$.

results.title: The maximum antichain size is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially ordered set. Some antichain in $\alpha$ has exactly as many elements as the maximum antichain size of $\alpha$.

results.title: The minimum chain cover size is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite partially ordered set. Some chain cover $C$ of $\alpha$, a finite set of chains of $\alpha$ whose union is $\alpha$, consists of exactly as many chains as the minimum chain cover size of $\alpha$.

results.title: Resource-allocation state
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: For a type $P$ of processes and a type $R$ of resource types, a state consists of two functions $\mathrm{alloc}, \mathrm{request} : P \to R \to \mathbb{N}$: $\mathrm{alloc}(p)(r)$ is the number of instances of resource type $r$ that process $p$ holds, and $\mathrm{request}(p)(r)$ is the number of instances of $r$ that $p$ is waiting for.

results.title: Reduction sequences
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $P$ be a type of processes and $R$ a type of resource types, and let $S$ be a state that gives each process $p$ an allocation $\mathrm{alloc}(p)$ and a request $\mathrm{request}(p)$, both functions $R \to \mathbb{N}$ ordered componentwise. A list of processes $p_1, \dots, p_k$ is a reduction sequence of $S$ from the free vector $w : R \to \mathbb{N}$ when, for every $1 \le i \le k$, we have…

results.title: Letting a process that fits finish first preserves reduction sequences
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be a resource vector and $p$ a process whose request is at most $w$. If $\sigma$ is a reduction sequence from $w$, then the list obtained from $\sigma$ by removing the first occurrence of $p$, if any, is a reduction sequence from $w$ plus the allocation of $p$.

results.title: A reduction sequence in which no process fits is empty
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be a resource vector. If $\sigma$ is a reduction sequence from $w$ and no process of $\sigma$ has a request at most $w$, then $\sigma$ is empty.

results.title: The detection algorithm with fuel
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given the fuel, a number of steps, together with the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, the algorithm returns two lists: the processes that finished, in order, and the processes left over. With fuel $0$, or when no pending process has a request at most $w$, no process finishes and all the pending processes are left over. Otherwise the fuel is $n + 1$ for some $n$; take the first pending…

results.title: The processes the detection algorithm lets finish
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, run the detection algorithm: repeatedly take the first pending process whose request is at most what is free, let it finish, remove that entry from the list and add its allocation to what is free, until no pending process has a request at most what is free. This is the list of the processes taken, in the order they were taken.

results.title: The detection algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given the free resource vector $w$ and a list of pending processes, repeatedly take the first pending process whose request is at most what is free, let it finish, remove that entry from the list and add its allocation to what is free, until no pending process has a request at most what is free. The processes still pending then are the ones reported as deadlocked.

results.title: The algorithm with fuel leaves over no process of a reduction sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector, let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates, and let the fuel be at least the number of pending processes. If $\sigma$ is a duplicate-free reduction sequence from $w$ all of whose processes are pending, then no process of $\sigma$ is among the processes that the detection algorithm with that fuel leaves over.

results.title: Every reported process is stuck
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector. For every process $q$ that the detection algorithm reports, the request of $q$ is not at most $w$ plus the sum of the allocations of the processes that the algorithm lets finish: for at least one resource type, $q$ requests more than is free even after all those processes have released their allocations.

results.title: The processes the algorithm lets finish form a reduction sequence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every free resource vector $w$ and every list of pending processes, the processes that the detection algorithm lets finish, in the order it lets them finish, form a reduction sequence from $w$.

results.title: Correctness of deadlock detection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector and let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates. A process $p$ is reported by the detection algorithm if and only if $p$ is pending and no duplicate-free reduction sequence $\sigma$ from $w$ made of pending processes contains $p$.

results.title: No deadlock is reported exactly when all the processes can finish
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be the free resource vector and let the list of pending processes contain no duplicates. The detection algorithm, started with $w$ free, reports no process if and only if some reordering of the pending processes is a reduction sequence from $w$.

results.title: Rate ratio at a given steady-state modified fraction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The value of `V₁ / V₂` for which the mole fraction `W` of modified protein is at steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 8): `W (1 - W + K₁) / ((1 - W) (W + K₂))`. Meaningful for `0 < W < 1` and `K₁, K₂ > 0`; at `W = 1` Lean's `a / 0 = 0` gives the junk value `0`.

results.title: Goldbeter–Koshland function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Goldbeter–Koshland function: the steady-state mole fraction of modified protein when `V₁ / V₂ = v` (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7, rationalized so that it also covers `v = 1`, Eq. 9). Meaningful for `v, K₁, K₂ > 0`.

results.title: Response coefficient of a covalent modification cycle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The response coefficient `R_v`: the ratio of the values of `V₁ / V₂` giving 90% and 10% modified protein at steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981).

results.title: Hill response function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The fraction of a Hill response `Sⁿ / (Kⁿ + Sⁿ)` with half-saturation constant `K` and Hill coefficient `n` (meaningful for `S, K > 0`, `n > 0`).

results.title: Steady state of the modification cycle
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Steady state of the modification cycle (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 8). For `V₂ > 0`, `K₁, K₂ > 0` and `0 < W < 1`, modification and demodification balance, `V₁ (1 - W) / (K₁ + 1 - W) = V₂ W / (K₂ + W)`, iff `V₁ / V₂ = rateRatio K₁ K₂ W`.

results.title: Rate ratio is strictly increasing in the modified fraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `rateRatio K₁ K₂` is strictly increasing on `(0, 1)` for `K₁, K₂ > 0`: it is the product of the positive increasing functions `W / (W + K₂)` and `1 + K₁ / (1 - W)`.

results.title: Goldbeter–Koshland function lies strictly between 0 and 1
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `v, K₁, K₂ > 0` the Goldbeter–Koshland function lies in `(0, 1)`.

results.title: The Goldbeter–Koshland function is a steady state
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Goldbeter–Koshland function is a steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7): for `v, K₁, K₂ > 0`, `rateRatio K₁ K₂ (goldbeterKoshland v K₁ K₂) = v`.

results.title: Uniqueness of the steady state
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Uniqueness of the steady state (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 7). For `K₁, K₂ > 0`, if `0 < W < 1` and `rateRatio K₁ K₂ W = v` with `v > 0`, then `W` is the Goldbeter–Koshland function.

results.title: Equal maximal rates
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Equal maximal rates (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 9): for `V₁ = V₂` and `K₁, K₂ > 0` the steady-state modified fraction is `K₂ / (K₁ + K₂)`.

results.title: The response coefficient
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The response coefficient (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 10): for `K₁, K₂ > -0.1`, `R_v = 81 (K₁ + 0.1)(K₂ + 0.1) / ((K₁ + 0.9)(K₂ + 0.9))`.

results.title: Response coefficient exceeds 1
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `K₁, K₂ > 0` the response coefficient exceeds `1`: the switch is never infinitely sharp.

results.title: Response coefficient is below the Michaelis–Menten value 81
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `K₁, K₂ > 0` the response coefficient is below the Michaelis–Menten value `81`.

results.title: First-order limit
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: As both `K₁, K₂ → ∞` the response coefficient tends to `81`, the value of a Michaelis–Menten response.

results.title: Zero-order ultrasensitivity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: As both `K₁, K₂ → 0` the response coefficient tends to `1`.

results.title: Hill response coefficient
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Hill response coefficient (Goldbeter–Koshland 1981, Eq. 11). For a Hill response with `n > 0` and `K > 0`, if `S₉, S₁ > 0` give 90% and 10% response, then `S₉ / S₁ = 81 ^ (1 / n)`.

results.title: Michaelis–Menten response
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Michaelis–Menten response (`n = 1`): going from 10% to 90% of the response takes an 81-fold increase of the stimulus.
